items.stem: What is meant by the luminosity of a star?
options: the surface temperature of the star
the total power of radiation emitted by the star
the brightness of the star seen from Earth
the power received per unit area at the Earth
items.answer: the total power of radiation emitted by the star
items.markingKey: Luminosity L in W.

items.stem: Explain how a standard candle is used to determine the distance to a galaxy.
items.answer: The luminosity L of the standard candle is known (e.g. from the period of a Cepheid); its radiant flux intensity F at the Earth is measured; then d = √(L/4πF).
items.markingKey: L known [1]; F measured, d = √(L/4πF) [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the radiant flux intensity from a star obeys an inverse-square law with distance.
items.answer: The power L spreads out uniformly over the surface of a sphere of area 4πd²; the intensity is power per unit area, so F = L/(4πd²) ∝ 1/d².
items.markingKey: power spreads over sphere 4πd² [1]; F ∝ 1/d² [1] [2]

items.stem: The star Arcturus has a luminosity of 6.51 × 10²⁸ W and is 8.6 light-years (8.14 × 10¹⁶ m) from the Earth. Work out the radiant flux intensity at the Earth.
items.markingKey: F = L/(4πd²) = 6.51 × 10²⁸/(4π × (8.14 × 10¹⁶)²) = 7.83 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The radiant flux intensity at the Earth from a Cepheid variable star of luminosity 1.68 × 10²⁹ W is 4.94 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻². Calculate its distance from the Earth in metres and in light-years (1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m).

A Cepheid variable star in a distant galaxy has a luminosity, deduced from its period, of 5.0 × 10³⁰ W. Its measured radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷ W m⁻². (a) State what is meant by a standard candle. (b) Calculate the distance to the galaxy. (c) Suggest one source of uncertainty in this distance.
items.answer: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity. (b) 1.26 × 10²³ m (c) Absorption by dust reduces F; uncertainty in the period–luminosity calibration.
items.markingKey: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity [1] (b) d = √(L/4πF) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.26 × 10²³ m [1] [2] (c) Absorption by dust reduces F; uncertainty in the period–luminosity calibration [1]

items.stem: What is meant by a standard candle?
options: the brightest star in a galaxy
an astronomical object of known luminosity
items.answer: an astronomical object of known luminosity
items.markingKey: Known L plus measured F gives d.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why are Type Ia supernovae useful for measuring the distances to distant galaxies? (b) What is meant by the luminosity of a star?
items.answer: (a) they have a known, very large peak luminosity (b) the total power of radiation emitted by the star
items.markingKey: (a) Bright enough to be seen at great distances. (b) Luminosity L in W.

items.stem: Suggest why different standard candles are needed for nearby and very distant galaxies.
items.answer: Cepheids are not bright enough to be seen in very distant galaxies; much more luminous standard candles such as Type Ia supernovae are needed there, calibrated using nearer Cepheid distances.
items.markingKey: Cepheids too faint at large d [1]; supernovae brighter [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the radiant flux intensity measured at the Earth may be smaller than L/(4πd²).
items.answer: Some radiation is absorbed or scattered by interstellar dust and gas and by the Earth's atmosphere, so less power reaches the detector.
items.markingKey: absorption/scattering by dust or atmosphere [1]; less power received [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Suggest why different standard candles are needed for nearby and very distant galaxies. (b) Explain how a standard candle is used to determine the distance to a galaxy.
items.answer: (a) Cepheids are not bright enough to be seen in very distant galaxies; much more luminous standard candles such as Type Ia supernovae are needed there, calibrated using nearer Cepheid distances. (b) The luminosity L of the standard candle is known (e.g. from the period of a Cepheid); its radiant flux intensity F at the Earth is measured; then d = √(L/4πF).
items.markingKey: (a) Cepheids too faint at large d [1]; supernovae brighter [1] [2] (b) L known [1]; F measured, d = √(L/4πF) [1] [2]

items.stem: The star Betelgeuse has a luminosity of 4.83 × 10³¹ W and is 250 light-years (2.37 × 10¹⁸ m) from the Earth. Work out the radiant flux intensity at the Earth.
items.markingKey: F = L/(4πd²) = 4.83 × 10³¹/(4π × (2.37 × 10¹⁸)²) = 6.87 × 10⁻⁷ W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The star Arcturus has a luminosity of 6.51 × 10²⁸ W and is 550 light-years (5.20 × 10¹⁸ m) from the Earth. Determine the radiant flux intensity at the Earth.
items.markingKey: F = L/(4πd²) = 6.51 × 10²⁸/(4π × (5.20 × 10¹⁸)²) = 1.91 × 10⁻¹⁰ W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The star Betelgeuse has a luminosity of 4.83 × 10³¹ W and is 860 light-years (8.14 × 10¹⁸ m) from the Earth. Work out the radiant flux intensity at the Earth.
items.markingKey: F = L/(4πd²) = 4.83 × 10³¹/(4π × (8.14 × 10¹⁸)²) = 5.80 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The Sun has luminosity 3.83 × 10²⁶ W and the radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 1.36 × 10³ W m⁻². The star Altair has a luminosity 10.6 times that of the Sun and a measured radiant flux intensity of 8.81 × 10⁻¹² W m⁻² at the Earth. (a) Calculate the Earth–Sun distance. (b) Calculate the distance to Altair. (c) Explain why this method requires the luminosity to be known independently.
items.answer: (a) 1.50 × 10¹¹ m (b) 6.05 × 10¹⁸ m (c) the measured F depends on both L and d; only if L is known (standard candle) can d be found
items.markingKey: (a) d = √(L/4πF) = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m [1] (b) L = 4.06 × 10²⁷ W [1]; d = 6.05 × 10¹⁸ m [1] (c) one equation, two unknowns [1]; L known for a standard candle [1] [5]

items.stem: A Cepheid variable star in a distant galaxy has a luminosity, deduced from its period, of 2.0 × 10³¹ W. Its measured radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ W m⁻². (a) State what is meant by a standard candle. (b) Calculate the distance to the galaxy.
items.answer: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity. (b) 1.99 × 10²³ m
items.markingKey: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity [1] (b) d = √(L/4πF) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.99 × 10²³ m [1] [2]

items.stem: A Cepheid variable star in a distant galaxy has a luminosity, deduced from its period, of 5.0 × 10³⁰ W. Its measured radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ W m⁻². (a) State what is meant by a standard candle. (b) Express this distance in megaparsecs (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m). (c) Explain why the luminosity of a Cepheid can be found from its period. (d) Suggest one source of uncertainty in this distance.
items.answer: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity. (b) 3.23 Mpc (c) Cepheids obey a period–luminosity relationship calibrated with nearby Cepheids of known distance. (d) Absorption by dust reduces F; uncertainty in the period–luminosity calibration.
items.markingKey: (a) An astronomical object of known luminosity [1] (b) ÷ 3.09 × 10²²: 3.23 Mpc [1] (c) Cepheids obey a period–luminosity relationship calibrated with nearby Cepheids of known distance [1] (d) Absorption by dust reduces F; uncertainty in the period–luminosity calibration [1]

(d) Suggest one source of uncertainty in this distance.

items.stem: Wien's displacement law states that the wavelength at which a black body emits maximum power is …
options: inversely proportional to its thermodynamic temperature
items.answer: inversely proportional to its thermodynamic temperature
items.markingKey: λmax ∝ 1/T.

items.stem: Explain how the radius of a star can be determined from observations.
items.answer: Measure λmax in its spectrum and use Wien's law to find T; find L (from F and d, or as a standard candle); then use L = 4πσr²T⁴ to calculate r.
items.markingKey: T from Wien's law [1]; r from Stefan–Boltzmann with L [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a red giant can be much more luminous than the Sun although its surface is cooler.
items.answer: L ∝ r²T⁴; although T is lower, its radius is very much larger, so r² more than compensates for the smaller T⁴.
items.markingKey: L = 4πσr²T⁴ [1]; much larger r compensates [1] [2]

items.stem: The star Altair has a surface temperature of 7670 K. Determine the wavelength at which its emission is a maximum.
items.markingKey: λmax = 2.9 × 10⁻³/T = 2.9 × 10⁻³/7670 = 3.78 × 10⁻⁷ m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The spectrum of Sirius A has its peak intensity at 2.92 × 10⁻⁷ m. Its luminosity is 9.73 × 10²⁷ W. Calculate its surface temperature and its radius.

Observations of Altair show that its spectrum peaks at 3.78 × 10⁻⁷ m and that its luminosity is 4.06 × 10²⁷ W. (a) State Wien's displacement law. (b) Calculate the surface temperature. (c) State one assumption made in these calculations.
items.answer: (a) λmax ∝ 1/T (λmax T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K). (b) 7670 K (c) The star is a black body (or a uniform sphere).
items.markingKey: (a) λmax ∝ 1/T (λmax T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K) [1] (b) T = 2.9 × 10⁻³/λmax (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7670 K with unit [1] [2] (c) The star is a black body (or a uniform sphere) [1]

items.stem: The Stefan–Boltzmann law for a star of radius r and surface temperature T is …
items.answer: L = 4πσr²T⁴
items.markingKey: Power = σ × area × T⁴.

items.stem: State the assumptions made when applying Wien's law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law to stars.
items.answer: The star behaves as a black body (perfect emitter) and is spherical with a uniform surface temperature.
items.markingKey: black body [1]; spherical/uniform temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Two stars are compared using the Stefan–Boltzmann law. The surface temperature is reduced to one third while the radius stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the luminosity of the star changes.
items.answer: The luminosity of the star is multiplied by 0.0123.
items.markingKey: Using L = 4πσr²T⁴: luminosity of the star ∝ surface temperature^4.00; factor = 0.333^4.00 = 0.0123. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A star is modelled as a black body. The radius is reduced to one third while the surface temperature stays the same. Explain how the luminosity of the star changes.
items.answer: The luminosity of the star becomes one ninth.
items.markingKey: Using L = 4πσr²T⁴: luminosity of the star ∝ radius^2.00; factor = 0.333^2.00 = 0.111. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State the assumptions made when applying Wien's law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law to stars. (b) Explain why a red giant can be much more luminous than the Sun although its surface is cooler.

items.stem: What is meant by redshift?
options: the decrease in wavelength from an approaching source
the absorption of blue light by dust
the increase in observed wavelength of radiation from a source moving away from the observer
the reddening of stars as they cool
items.answer: the increase in observed wavelength of radiation from a source moving away from the observer
items.markingKey: Δλ/λ ≈ v/c for v ≪ c.

items.stem: Explain how Hubble's law supports the Big Bang theory.
items.answer: All distant galaxies are receding with speeds proportional to their distances, so the Universe is expanding; tracing the expansion back in time implies that everything was once concentrated at a single point and has been expanding since.
items.markingKey: universe expanding [1]; extrapolate back to a single point/origin [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the recession speed of a galaxy is found from its spectrum.
items.answer: Identify a known spectral line, measure its observed wavelength and compare with the laboratory wavelength: Δλ/λ = v/c, so v = cΔλ/λ.
items.markingKey: compare observed and laboratory wavelength [1]; v = cΔλ/λ [1] [2]

items.stem: The calcium K line has a wavelength of 393.4 nm in the laboratory. In the spectrum of a distant galaxy it is observed at 396.5 nm. Calculate the speed of recession of the galaxy.
items.markingKey: v = cΔλ/λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 3.10/393.4 = 2.36 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The hydrogen-beta line has a wavelength of 486.1 nm in the laboratory. In the spectrum of a distant galaxy it is observed at 491.9 nm. Taking H₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹, calculate the recession speed and the distance to the galaxy.

The hydrogen-alpha line has a wavelength of 656.3 nm in the laboratory. In the spectrum of a distant galaxy it is observed at 664.2 nm. Take H₀ = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the recession speed. (b) Calculate the distance to the galaxy in Mpc (1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m). (c) Use H₀ to estimate the age of the Universe in years (1 year = 3.16 × 10⁷ s).
items.answer: (a) 3.61 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (b) 48.7 Mpc (c) 1.32 × 10¹⁰ years

items.stem: In the spectrum of a distant galaxy the sodium D line (laboratory wavelength 589 nm) is observed at 647.9 nm. The Hubble constant is 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the recession speed. (b) Explain how Hubble's law leads to the idea of the Big Bang.
items.answer: (a) 3.00 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ (b) Galaxies receding with v ∝ d means the Universe is expanding; running time backwards, all matter was once together at one point.
items.markingKey: (a) v = cΔλ/λ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.00 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) expansion [1]; common origin [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the age of the Universe estimated from 1/H₀ is only approximate.
items.answer: It assumes that the expansion rate has been constant since the Big Bang; in fact it has changed (slowed by gravity, accelerated by dark energy), and H₀ itself has uncertainty.
items.markingKey: assumes constant expansion rate [1]; uncertainty in H₀ / rate has changed [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why it does not mean that the Earth is at the centre of the Universe when all distant galaxies are seen to be moving away from us.
items.answer: Space itself is expanding uniformly; an observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies receding with v ∝ d, so there is no special centre.
items.markingKey: uniform expansion of space [1]; same view from any galaxy [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how a standard candle is used to determine the distance to a galaxy. (b) Explain why the radiant flux intensity from a star obeys an inverse-square law with distance.
items.answer: (a) The luminosity L of the standard candle is known (e.g. from the period of a Cepheid); its radiant flux intensity F at the Earth is measured; then d = √(L/4πF). (b) The power L spreads out uniformly over the surface of a sphere of area 4πd²; the intensity is power per unit area, so F = L/(4πd²) ∝ 1/d².
items.markingKey: (a) L known [1]; F measured, d = √(L/4πF) [1] [2] (b) power spreads over sphere 4πd² [1]; F ∝ 1/d² [1] [2]

items.stem: A Type Ia supernova in a distant galaxy is observed. The luminosity is increased by 50% while the distance from the Earth stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the radiant flux intensity received at the Earth changes.
items.answer: The radiant flux intensity received at the Earth increases by 50%.
items.markingKey: Using F = L/(4πd²): radiant flux intensity received at the Earth ∝ luminosity; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: The star Rigel has a luminosity of 4.60 × 10³¹ W and is 8.6 light-years (8.14 × 10¹⁶ m) from the Earth. Determine the radiant flux intensity at the Earth.
items.markingKey: F = L/(4πd²) = 4.60 × 10³¹/(4π × (8.14 × 10¹⁶)²) = 5.53 × 10⁻⁴ W m⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The radiant flux intensity at the Earth from a Cepheid variable star of luminosity 4.60 × 10³¹ W is 6.54 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻². Calculate its distance from the Earth in metres and in light-years (1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m).

A Cepheid variable star in a distant galaxy has a luminosity, deduced from its period, of 5.0 × 10³⁰ W. Its measured radiant flux intensity at the Earth is 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁷ W m⁻². (a) Calculate the distance to the galaxy. (b) Explain why the luminosity of a Cepheid can be found from its period. (c) Suggest one source of uncertainty in this distance.
items.answer: (a) 1.26 × 10²³ m (b) Cepheids obey a period–luminosity relationship calibrated with nearby Cepheids of known distance. (c) Absorption by dust reduces F; uncertainty in the period–luminosity calibration.

Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a red giant can be much more luminous than the Sun although its surface is cooler. (b) State the assumptions made when applying Wien's law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law to stars.
items.answer: (a) L ∝ r²T⁴; although T is lower, its radius is very much larger, so r² more than compensates for the smaller T⁴. (b) The star behaves as a black body (perfect emitter) and is spherical with a uniform surface temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) L = 4πσr²T⁴ [1]; much larger r compensates [1] [2] (b) black body [1]; spherical/uniform temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how the radius of a star can be determined from observations. (b) State the assumptions made when applying Wien's law and the Stefan–Boltzmann law to stars.
items.answer: (a) Measure λmax in its spectrum and use Wien's law to find T; find L (from F and d, or as a standard candle); then use L = 4πσr²T⁴ to calculate r. (b) The star behaves as a black body (perfect emitter) and is spherical with a uniform surface temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) T from Wien's law [1]; r from Stefan–Boltzmann with L [1] [2] (b) black body [1]; spherical/uniform temperature [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which observation is evidence that the Universe is expanding? (b) State Hubble's law.
items.answer: (a) light from distant galaxies is redshifted by amounts that increase with distance (b) The recession speed of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance from us (v = H₀d).
items.markingKey: (a) Cosmological redshift ∝ distance. (b) v ∝ d [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why it does not mean that the Earth is at the centre of the Universe when all distant galaxies are seen to be moving away from us. (b) Explain how Hubble's law supports the Big Bang theory.
items.answer: (a) Space itself is expanding uniformly; an observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies receding with v ∝ d, so there is no special centre. (b) All distant galaxies are receding with speeds proportional to their distances, so the Universe is expanding; tracing the expansion back in time implies that everything was once concentrated at a single point and has been expanding since.
items.markingKey: (a) uniform expansion of space [1]; same view from any galaxy [1] [2] (b) universe expanding [1]; extrapolate back to a single point/origin [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the age of the Universe estimated from 1/H₀ is only approximate. (b) Explain why it does not mean that the Earth is at the centre of the Universe when all distant galaxies are seen to be moving away from us.
items.answer: (a) It assumes that the expansion rate has been constant since the Big Bang; in fact it has changed (slowed by gravity, accelerated by dark energy), and H₀ itself has uncertainty. (b) Space itself is expanding uniformly; an observer in any galaxy would see all other galaxies receding with v ∝ d, so there is no special centre.
items.markingKey: (a) assumes constant expansion rate [1]; uncertainty in H₀ / rate has changed [1] [2] (b) uniform expansion of space [1]; same view from any galaxy [1] [2]
